appraisal_events.evidence: « la demoiselle de Robert, je vous assure qu’elle est à mourir de rire » ; « Robert a peut-être l’ivresse, mais il n’a vraiment pas fait preuve de goût dans le choix du flacon ! » ; l’anecdote de l’escalier au milieu du salon et des Sept Princesses.
appraisal_events.explanation: The duchesse demolishes Saint-Loup's mistress before an appreciative salon, turning her pretensions and her taste in theatre into a sustained comic exhibit, and in the same breath convicts Robert of bad taste for choosing her.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Quelle buse ! » pensais-je, irrité de l’accueil glacial qu’elle m’avait fait. Je trouvais une sorte d’âpre satisfaction à constater sa complète incompréhension de Maeterlinck. […] « Maintenant c’est moi qui ne voudrais pas d’elle. » Tels étaient les mots que je me disais ; ils étaient le contraire de ma pensée.
appraisal_events.explanation: After her icy reception, the narrator convicts the duchesse of philistine incomprehension — a charge the narrating voice leaves standing through the verb « constater » — but immediately unmasks his own contempt as insincere self-consolation, so the diminishment also recoils on him.

status_effects.explanation: She is made the object of extended salon ridicule — ludicrous, pretentious, and artistically absurd — with no voice or defence in the passage.
The Augier gibe about the flacon explicitly impugns Robert's taste and judgment through the woman he has chosen.
She holds the floor with sustained mockery that lands: d'Argencourt laughs and takes up her theme, while the historian's competing witticism goes entirely unheard.
Against her salon success, the narration registers her boasted ignorance of Maeterlinck as genuine incomprehension, lowering her as a judge of art even as her wit prevails socially.
He has been coldly received, and his retaliatory contempt is exposed as agitated, insincere talk that only confirms his dependence on a woman for whom he walks kilometres every morning.

ambiguities: « la demoiselle de Robert » is never named in the passage; identifying her with Rachel rests on the reference sheet and on Robert being named, so the direct target of the duchesse's mockery is resolved by inference rather than by the text.

The narrator's verdict on the duchesse is explicitly disavowed (« ils étaient le contraire de ma pensée », « de purs mots de conversation »), yet « constater sa complète incompréhension de Maeterlinck » leaves the factual charge intact; it is genuinely underdetermined how far the narration endorses her diminishment versus turning the irony wholly back on the narrator.
